paras: The reported lynching of Jim Brown and "Blind Jim" at Flagstaff was the hanging, announced in July 1882, of two men accused of shooting two residents of Flagstaff, then in Arizona Territory though wire reports placed it in New Mexico. Wire dispatches said the whole town had caught and hanged them, and the item entered a year-end chronology as "Two murderers lynched at Flagstaff, N. M." Weeks later, however, Blind Jim was arrested alive in Kansas, and he was acquitted of murder at Prescott that winter.

According to the Weekly Arizona Miner of Prescott, on 6 July a man named Brown, "a sport," and his partner killed a man named Stone "for some frivolous offense," along with an onlooker named Deitrich. An Albuquerque dispatch of 7 July described the shooting as a quarrel and named the gunmen as Blind Jim and Jim Brown and the dead as Storey and Deitrich. Later papers called Stone or Storey a contractor for the Atlantic and Pacific railroad.

The two men fled to the woods, and a Denver dispatch said nearly the whole town was in pursuit and that "when caught they will be hanged to the nearest tree." The Miner reported that the citizens followed them and that "the last seen of them they were swinging to a pine limb, stark dead," though it was unsure of the partner's name, giving it as "Benjamine" with the words "we believe." A Santa Fe wire of 11 July likewise said the whole town "pursued, caught and hanged the murderers."

On 7 August Jim Paxton, "alias Blind Jim," was arrested at Larned, Kansas, for killing Storey at Flagstaff and held for Arizona officers. The Miner then explained that he had fled east to his father's home in Pawnee County, "although it was reported that the citizens of Flagstaff had hanged him and his partner." Deputy Sheriff William Mulvenon brought him back alone, leaving the train and crossing the country by private conveyance after learning that friends planned a rescue and that others along the road meant to lynch him.

By 1 December the Phoenix Herald reported that "Blind Jim," properly James Paxton, had been acquitted at Prescott of the murder of F. H. Stone. No later report on Jim Brown, the recovery of a body, or an inquest appears in the coverage.

The hanging reached national readers through a Santa Fe special, printed in Memphis as "Murderers Lynched," in Wheeling as "Murderers Strung Up" and in Burlington, Vermont, as "Two Desperadoes Lynched," the last adding that the killings came in "a street fight." Weekly news digests in Dakota and Iowa repeated it in one line, and the Las Vegas Gazette had anticipated the outcome by joking that the shooters were by then "interviewing Guiteau."

None of these papers questioned the hanging or mentioned the race of any of the men, and the Miner described the dead as "inoffensive, good citizens." The correction came only in Arizona papers, while a Michigan year-end review in late December still listed the episode as a double lynching in New Mexico.

The papers disagree on whether the lynching happened: the July reports say both men were hanged, while the August, September and December Arizona reports show Blind Jim alive, jailed and tried. The date also varies, from 6 July in the Arizona papers to "this morning" in a 7 July wire and "yesterday" in an 11 July wire.

reader.title: Reported lynching of Jim Brown and "Blind Jim" at Flagstaff
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Wire and territorial reports said citizens pursued and hanged two men accused of a double killing (A6, A8, A9), though one of the two was later found alive (A11, A12).

July reports said the 'whole town' or the citizens hanged Jim Brown and Blind Jim for a double murder (A6, A9), but Blind Jim was arrested alive in Kansas and later acquitted (A11, A12, A13), and the Miner called the hanging only a report (A12); no later item confirms that Brown was killed. Nothing in the coverage gives the race of anyone involved.
Several wire and territorial reports of the hanging (A6, A8, A9) are contradicted for Blind Jim by his arrest, return and trial (A11, A12, A13), and no independent report confirms Brown's death.

framing.detail: National papers ran the Santa Fe wire under 'Murderers Lynched' and 'Murderers Strung Up', calling the accused murderers and desperadoes without comment on the mob.
The Las Vegas Gazette joked that the shooters were by then 'interviewing Guiteau'.

The Prescott Miner first reported the hanging as news and praised the victims, then in September called Blind Jim 'the notorious Flagstaff murderer' and praised the deputy who kept him from lynchers and rescuers.
